text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meets on Tuesday, July 1.

Ahead of the meeting, Reuters asked 26 economists what chance they saw of a rate cut during July, and if there was no rate cut in the month, what chance they saw of there being another cut after July.
The median results show a slightly better than even chance of a July cut, falling back to a 50/50 proposition afterwards, but the results disguise a number of varied opinions.
The RBA can cut rates on any day it chooses, meaning that Governor Ian Macfarlane can be given the discretion to ease on any day up to the next meeting on August 5.

For that reason, economists felt an easing next Wednesday morning, the first opportunity after the July board meeting, was unlikely, as the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee will still be meeting and it could possibly raise rates on Thursday morning Australian time.

Economists felt if the RBA had decided to ease, it would wait to see what the FOMC did, just to make sure it did not startle markets, which meant an announcement was seen as more likely on Thursday rather than Wednesday.

If the FOMC raises rates, it was seen delaying a local move to give markets time to adjust to local official rates being below those of the U.S., while no move by the FOMC would leave Thursday as an opportunity for a local easing.
However, on Wednesday May retail trade data is expected to show a strong rise, and employment data the following week is also expected to rebound strongly after a weak figure for May.

While this would not change the picture of a still sluggish economy, some felt the RBA may wait until second quarter inflation and wages data due on July 23 and 24 respectively to boltster the case for a rate cut.

The inflation data is expected to show the consumer price index coming in under 1.0 percent in annual terms and the annual underlying rate dropping below two percent. As well, the wages data is expected to confirm that wage settlements are not running at a pace threatening inflation.

On this reasoning, an easing would be held off until late July, or after the August 5 board meeting, as the RBA could then present a solid case of falling inflation and wages as support for a rate cut.
However, if a cut had not occurred after the August board meeting, a number of economists said the odds on another would then lengthen.
